query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a thin, well‐bonded high-quality graphene interlayer on tungsten particles before copper infiltration will lower the interfacial thermal resistance in W–Cu composites, thereby increasing overall thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional W–Cu composite produced by standard powder metallurgy or infiltration methods using untreated tungsten particles.
generation.intervention: Apply a conformal graphene coating on tungsten particles prior to copper infiltration.
generation.conditions: The intervention is expected to work under high heat-dissipation conditions and in fusion-reactor joint applications, including exposure to elevated temperatures and moderate neutron irradiation typical of reactor environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The graphene interlayer serves as an engineered interface between tungsten and copper, facilitating improved phonon and electron coupling across the interface.
generation.mechanism: Graphene has an extremely high in-plane thermal conductivity. When used as a nanolayer at the tungsten-copper interface, it reduces thermal boundary resistance by providing an efficient pathway for heat transfer. Its intrinsic strength and chemical stability should also help preserve mechanical integrity and irradiation resistance by maintaining robust interfacial bonding and mitigating stress concentrations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with an otherwise identical untreated W–Cu composite, the graphene-coated composite is expected to exhibit a measurable increase in overall thermal conductivity, while mechanical properties and irradiation resistance remain at least equivalent to the baseline.
generation.baseline: Performance of conventional W–Cu composites fabricated without any interfacial modifications.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds provided that the graphene coating maintains its integrity under operating temperatures and irradiation doses typical of fusion reactors; excessive interfacial degradation or delamination would limit these benefits.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the long-term chemical stability and bonding quality of the graphene interlayer under prolonged irradiation exposure and thermal cycling, which may affect the durability of the enhanced interface.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composites: one set with tungsten particles pre-coated with a high-quality graphene interlayer using chemical vapor deposition (or an equivalent method) and one set using the standard process without graphene. Subject both sets to standardized thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., laser flash analysis), mechanical durability tests (e.g., cyclic loading and fracture toughness), and controlled irradiation tests mimicking the neutron flux of fusion reactors.
measurements: Overall thermal conductivity across a range of temperatures
Mechanical properties such as tensile strength, fracture toughness, and fatigue resistance
Interfacial integrity and microstructural stability pre- and post-irradiation via microscopy and spectroscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the graphene-coated composites do not show a statistically significant improvement in thermal conductivity over the uncoated composites, or if they exhibit a measurable reduction in mechanical durability or irradiation resistance under the simulated application conditions, the hypothesis would be falsified.
